Schoolmen
skōōl´mĕn
n. pl. (the scholastic theologians of the medieval universities)
School + men: the masters of the cathedral and university schools, from the twelfth to the fifteenth centuries — Lombard, Aquinas, Scotus, Occam — whose method is called scholasticism.

Biblical Definition

The schoolmen are the theologians of the medieval schools, and Calvin's Institutes argue with them on nearly every page. Their method was rigorous and their distinctions are still useful; their error, as the Reformers saw it, was to let Aristotle set the questions Scripture had not asked, and to build doctrine on inference where the text was silent. Paul's warning is the standing caution: “Beware lest any man spoil you through philosophy and vain deceit, after the tradition of men, after the rudiments of the world, and not after Christ” (Col 2:8), and to Timothy, “avoid foolish and unlearned questions, knowing that they do gender strifes” (2Ti 2:23).

Webster 1828 Definition

Webster (1828) defines schoolman as one versed in the niceties of academical disputation or of school divinity; a writer of scholastic divinity.

expand to see more

SCHOOLMAN, n. A man versed in the niceties of academical disputation or of school divinity.

2. A writer of scholastic divinity or philosophy.

Key Scripture

Col 2:8 — "Beware lest any man spoil you through philosophy and vain deceit, after the tradition of men, after the rudiments of the world, and not after Christ."

2Ti 2:23 — "But foolish and unlearned questions avoid, knowing that they do gender strifes."

1Ti 6:20 — "O Timothy, keep that which is committed to thy trust, avoiding profane and vain babblings, and oppositions of science falsely so called:"

1Co 1:20 — "Where is the wise? where is the scribe? where is the disputer of this world? hath not God made foolish the wisdom of this world?"

2Ti 2:14 — "Of these things put them in remembrance, charging them before the Lord that they strive not about words to no profit, but to the subverting of the hearers."

Modern Corruption

Scholastic care is dismissed as dead precision, and the men who most despise it usually have no doctrine precise enough to defend.

expand to see more

The Reformers were not anti-intellectual and did not despise the schoolmen wholesale; Calvin quotes Lombard and Bernard with respect and reserves his sharpness for what he thinks is sophistry. The complaint is specific: that a method built for logic was made to govern revelation, so that a distinction skilfully drawn could establish a doctrine Scripture never taught — purgatory, the treasury of merit, transubstantiation defended by substance and accident. Colossians 2:8 does not forbid thinking; it forbids being carried off as spoil by a system whose first principles came from somewhere other than Christ.

The modern corruption runs the other way, and it is now the commoner one. A church that has never learned to define its terms calls the discipline of definition dry, prefers testimony to doctrine, and then finds it has no means of telling a heresy from a hymn. The scholastics' vices are unavailable to men who have not attained their virtues. The Reformed answer was not less precision but better warranted precision — the confessions themselves are scholastic in form, carefully articled and closely worded, and they are that way because the men who wrote them had watched loose language cost lives.

Greek & Hebrew Roots

Greek philosophia (G5385), philosophy; kenodoxia and apate (G539), deceit; zetesis (G2214), a questioning, disputation; logomacheo (G3054), to strive about words.

expand to see more

Greek philosophia (G5385) — philosophy; Colossians 2:8 only, with apate (G539), deceit.

Greek zetesis (G2214) — questioning, dispute; 2 Timothy 2:23, 1 Timothy 6:4, Titus 3:9.

Greek logomacheo (G3054) — to strive about words; 2 Timothy 2:14; antithesis (G477), oppositions; 1 Timothy 6:20.

Usage

"“Spoil you through philosophy and vain deceit” — carried off as plunder by a borrowed system."

"“Foolish and unlearned questions… gender strifes” — the vice of the method."

"“Oppositions of science falsely so called” — Paul's phrase for a learning that misses."
